vignette:
Liam is a 21-year-old white American man who came to treatment several months after a violent injury to a close family member, an event he still cannot tell in a smooth, ordinary way. When he tries, his speech stalls and fragments. He circles around it, then goes quiet, as if the experience exists in hard snapshots rather than a story. What comes most clearly are images: a particular part of his loved one's body after the injury, fixed in his mind with a cruel sharpness, "like photographs," and the smell that was in the air at the time, which returns so vividly that for a moment he feels he is back there again rather than remembering from a distance.

Since then, Liam has lived with a sense that danger can break through at any moment. If someone nearby moves suddenly, he is on guard before he has time to think. In those moments his body reacts fast and completely, and he has come to believe with bitterness that his body is no longer on his side. Even when he knows where he is, even when his wife tells him he is safe, his heart and muscles respond as if the emergency is still unfolding. What frightens him is not only the reaction itself but what it seems to say about him. He has begun to think he cannot rely on himself anymore, that some basic steadiness is gone.

The triggers in daily life are painfully specific. Seeing body parts associated with the injury can stop him cold; he finds his attention locking onto them before he can look away. Comments about family can do the same, especially casual remarks that would once have passed without notice. He hears them as loaded now, as if they could open the whole scene again. People who seem suspicious to him-someone watching too closely, lingering, moving unpredictably-make him tense immediately. Because he is unemployed, he spends much of his time in ordinary public and domestic settings where these moments catch him off guard: a stranger shifting abruptly in a checkout line, a neighbor making an offhand family comment, a scene in a waiting room where his eyes land on the wrong physical detail. The world feels full of traps he cannot reliably anticipate.

At times the past does not feel past. He describes sudden episodes in which it is as though the event is happening again. He may freeze, stare, or react to what is in his mind rather than what is around him. Afterwards he is shaken and ashamed. The smell from the original event can return during these episodes, which makes them feel even more real. At night he struggles to fall asleep and often cannot stay asleep. The dark and quiet do not bring rest; instead they leave him alone with the possibility of being pulled back into those images. Over time he has become wary of being alone in a room or building at all. He waits for his wife to come home, follows her from room to room, or keeps himself near other people because solitude feels too exposed.

He has also narrowed his life in quieter ways. He avoids television programs, films, and news stories that might resemble what happened. What used to be casual background entertainment now feels dangerous, as if one unexpected scene could overwhelm him. These habits have made his days smaller. Being unemployed has left him without the routines that once helped define him, and he now speaks as if that version of himself has been lost. He says he is no longer capable of doing the things that defined him, though he says this less as a dramatic statement than as a conclusion he has drawn from repeated moments of freezing, panicking, and withdrawing.

When the feelings crest and he cannot settle them, Liam sometimes hurts himself physically to release the pressure. He describes it as a way to cut through the unbearable build-up in his body when he feels overwhelmed. He does not present this as wanting to die, but as a desperate attempt to get temporary control over sensations that otherwise seem to own him.

His marriage has become both a comfort and a strain. His wife has seen how rarely he can be by himself now, how quickly a stranger's sudden movement can change his whole demeanor, how a remark about family can make him go silent and distant. What finally brought him in was the growing sense that his world was shrinking around these reactions and that he was becoming someone he did not recognize. He wants help making sense of what happened, especially because he still feels unable to put it into words. Most of all, he is afraid that this is permanent-that he will remain watchful, unreliable to himself, and unable to return to the life he thought was his.
